trap_notes.b: Privileges and Immunities bars states from discriminating against out-of-state citizens.
trap_notes.c: The Take Care Clause in Article II directs the president to enforce federal laws.
trap_notes.d: The Emoluments Clause bars officials from accepting foreign gifts or titles.
trap_notes.default: The Commerce Clause covers trade among the states and with foreign nations.

prompt: Identify this constitutional principle.
clues: It holds that government authority comes from the consent of the governed, not a monarch.
The Preamble expresses this idea immediately in its opening three words: 'We the People.'
Voters exercise it by electing representatives and amending state and national charters.

options.text: Popular sovereignty
Executive privilege
Judicial restraint
Parliamentary supremacy

explanation: Popular sovereignty means ultimate political authority rests with the people.

trap_notes.b: Executive privilege shields certain confidential presidential communications.
trap_notes.c: Judicial restraint encourages judges to defer to elected lawmakers.
trap_notes.d: Parliamentary supremacy places supreme power in a legislature, as in Britain.
trap_notes.default: Popular sovereignty roots government legitimacy in the consent of the people.

prompt: Identify this congressional procedure.
clues: It occurs in the U.S. Senate because its rules allow extended debate on most bills.
A senator or group can delay a floor vote by holding the floor or withholding consent.
Under Senate Rule XXII, ending this tactic usually requires a 60-vote cloture motion.

options.text: A Senate filibuster
A discharge petition
A presidential pocket veto
A continuing resolution

explanation: A Senate filibuster uses unlimited debate to block or delay a vote unless 60 senators invoke cloture.

trap_notes.b: A discharge petition forces a bill out of a House committee to the floor.
trap_notes.c: A pocket veto is a presidential action at the end of a congressional session.
trap_notes.d: A continuing resolution temporarily funds federal agencies.
trap_notes.default: Only the Senate allows filibusters, which require 60 votes for cloture.

prompt: Identify this legislative body.
clues: It is convened only when the House and Senate pass different versions of the same bill.
Members from both chambers meet temporarily to negotiate a single compromise text.
Once it agrees on a report, both the House and Senate must pass it without amendment.

options.text: A conference committee
A select intelligence committee
The House Rules Committee
The Electoral Commission

explanation: A conference committee resolves differences between House and Senate bills so identical text goes to the president.

trap_notes.b: Select committees investigate specific issues or oversee intelligence agencies.
trap_notes.c: The House Rules Committee sets debate terms only for the House floor.
trap_notes.d: The Electoral Commission was a one-time 1877 body for the 1876 election.
trap_notes.default: Conference committees reconcile differing House and Senate versions of a bill.

prompt: Identify this constitutional amendment.
clues: Ratified in 1967, it clarified presidential succession and disability procedures.
It allows the president to nominate a new vice president when that office falls vacant.
Gerald Ford and Nelson Rockefeller became vice president under its Section 2 process.

options.text: The Twenty-fifth Amendment
The Twentieth Amendment
The Twenty-second Amendment
The Twelfth Amendment

explanation: The 25th Amendment handles presidential disability and fills vice-presidential vacancies with congressional approval.

trap_notes.b: The 20th Amendment (1933) moved Inauguration Day from March 4 to January 20.
trap_notes.c: The 22nd Amendment (1951) limited presidents to two elected terms.
trap_notes.d: The 12th Amendment (1804) separated Electoral College votes for president and VP.
trap_notes.default: The 25th Amendment governs presidential disability and VP vacancies.

prompt: Identify this congressional check on the executive branch.
clues: It is a formal accusation of treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.
A simple majority vote in the House of Representatives brings the formal charges.
Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and Donald Trump faced this process, though none were removed.

options.text: House impeachment
Legislative censure
State recall vote
Writ of mandamus

explanation: The House impeaches by majority vote, and a two-thirds Senate vote is required for conviction and removal.

trap_notes.b: Censure is a formal reprimand that does not trigger a removal trial.
trap_notes.c: Recall elections exist in some states, not for federal officials.
trap_notes.d: A writ of mandamus is a court order compelling an official to perform a duty.
trap_notes.default: Impeachment is the House's formal charge, followed by a Senate trial.

prompt: Identify this model of U.S. federalism.
clues: It emerged during the Great Depression and New Deal as Washington expanded domestic aid.
Scholars compare it to a 'marble cake' because federal and state roles overlap.
Highway funding, Medicaid, and education grants all rely on shared federal-state administration.

options.text: Cooperative federalism
Dual-sphere federalism
Confederal unionism
Unitary centralism

explanation: Cooperative federalism ('marble cake') blends national and state authority through shared grants and programs.

trap_notes.b: Dual federalism ('layer cake') kept federal and state spheres strictly separate.
trap_notes.c: Confederalism gives supreme power to member states over a weak center.
trap_notes.d: Unitary centralism concentrates all constitutional power in a national government.
trap_notes.default: Cooperative federalism blends national and state duties like a marble cake.

prompt: Identify this federalism policy issue.
clues: State and local officials frequently criticize it as an unfair federal burden.
Congress imposes a legal requirement on states without providing money to pay for it.
Congress passed a 1995 reform act requiring cost estimates for bills that impose these rules.

options.text: Unfunded mandates
Block aid grants
Revenue sharing
Interstate compacts

explanation: Unfunded mandates require states or cities to follow federal rules without supplying matching federal funds.

trap_notes.b: Block grants provide federal money to states with broad spending flexibility.
trap_notes.c: Revenue sharing distributed federal tax dollars to states without narrow strings.
trap_notes.d: Interstate compacts are voluntary agreements between states approved by Congress.
trap_notes.default: Unfunded mandates impose federal duties on states without federal funding.

prompt: Identify this constitutional protection.
clues: It is found in the Fifth Amendment alongside due process and grand jury rights.
It allows government to take private land for public use such as highways or schools.
In return, the government must pay the owner 'just compensation' at fair market value.

options.text: Eminent domain
Double jeopardy
Habeas corpus
Ex post facto law

explanation: The Takings Clause recognizes eminent domain for public use while requiring just compensation.

trap_notes.b: Double jeopardy bars trying someone twice for the same crime.
trap_notes.c: Habeas corpus requires jailers to justify holding a prisoner before a judge.
trap_notes.d: Ex post facto laws retroactively punish past actions and are banned in Article I.
trap_notes.default: Eminent domain lets government acquire private property for public use with fair payment.

prompt: Identify this Reconstruction-era amendment.
clues: Ratified in 1870, it was the third and final Reconstruction Amendment.
It barred federal and state governments from denying the vote based on race or color.
Its promise was undermined by Jim Crow laws until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

options.text: The Fifteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Seventeenth Amendment

explanation: The 15th Amendment (1870) prohibited racial discrimination in voting, though enforcement lagged for nearly a century.

trap_notes.b: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery nationwide.
trap_notes.c: The 19th Amendment (1920) prohibited denying the vote based on sex.
trap_notes.d: The 17th Amendment (1913) established direct popular election of U.S. senators.
trap_notes.default: The 15th Amendment barred racial voting discrimination in 1870.

prompt: Identify this constitutional writ.
clues: Article I, Section 9 forbids suspending it except in cases of rebellion or invasion.
Its Latin name translates to 'you shall have the body.'
It lets a prisoner petition a court to test whether their detention is lawful.

options.text: Writ of habeas corpus
Bill of attainder
Writ of certiorari
Subpoena duces tecum

explanation: Habeas corpus protects against unlawful imprisonment by forcing officials to justify detention in court.

trap_notes.b: A bill of attainder is a banned legislative act punishing a person without trial.
trap_notes.c: A writ of certiorari is an order by a higher court to review a lower court case.
trap_notes.d: A subpoena orders a witness or documents to appear in court.
trap_notes.default: Habeas corpus lets detainees challenge unlawful imprisonment before a judge.

prompt: Identify this voting rights amendment.
clues: Leaders like Susan B. Anthony and Alice Paul campaigned for decades to win it.
Tennessee provided the decisive 36th state ratification in August 1920.
It barred federal and state governments from denying the vote on account of sex.

options.text: The Nineteenth Amendment
The Eighteenth Amendment
The Sixteenth Amendment
The Twenty-first Amendment

explanation: Ratified in 1920, the 19th Amendment secured women's suffrage nationwide.

trap_notes.b: The 18th Amendment (1919) enacted national Prohibition of alcohol.
trap_notes.c: The 16th Amendment (1913) authorized the federal income tax.
trap_notes.d: The 21st Amendment (1933) repealed national Prohibition.
trap_notes.default: The 19th Amendment (1920) guaranteed women's right to vote.

prompt: Identify this landmark Supreme Court case.
clues: The 1966 ruling grew out of a Phoenix police interrogation without a lawyer present.
The Court held that custodial questioning creates pressure against the Fifth Amendment.
Police must now warn suspects of their right to remain silent and to have an attorney.

options.text: Miranda v. Arizona
Gideon v. Wainwright
Mapp v. State of Ohio
Terry v. State of Ohio

explanation: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) created the required warnings before custodial police interrogation.

trap_notes.b: Gideon (1963) guaranteed appointed lawyers at felony trials, not police warnings.
trap_notes.c: Mapp (1961) barred illegally seized physical evidence in state trials.
trap_notes.d: Terry (1968) allowed brief police stop-and-frisk based on reasonable suspicion.
trap_notes.default: Miranda v. Arizona requires police to advise suspects of their rights before questioning.

prompt: Identify this landmark First Amendment case.
clues: The dispute began over a short, non-denominational prayer written by New York officials.
Public school students were asked to recite it aloud at the start of each day.
In 1962, the Supreme Court ruled state-composed school prayer violates the Establishment Clause.

options.text: Engel v. Vitale
Wisconsin v. Yoder
Tinker v. Des Moines
Schenck v. U.S.

explanation: Engel v. Vitale (1962) struck down official school-sponsored prayer even when students could opt out.

trap_notes.b: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) exempted Amish families from compulsory high school.
trap_notes.c: Tinker (1969) protected students' silent antiwar armband protest.
trap_notes.d: Schenck (1919) upheld limits on anti-draft leaflets during World War I.
trap_notes.default: Engel v. Vitale banned government-written prayers in public schools.

prompt: Identify this landmark separation-of-powers case.
clues: A special prosecutor subpoenaed Oval Office audio recordings during the Watergate scandal.
The president claimed absolute executive privilege to withhold the tapes from court.
In 1974, a unanimous Supreme Court ruled that no president is above criminal subpoenas.

options.text: United States v. Nixon
Youngstown Co. v. Sawyer
New York Times v. U.S.
Marbury v. Madison

explanation: United States v. Nixon (1974) forced the release of the Watergate tapes, affirming the rule of law.

trap_notes.b: Youngstown (1952) barred President Truman from seizing steel mills during the Korean War.
trap_notes.c: New York Times Co. v. United States (1971) blocked prior restraint on the Pentagon Papers.
trap_notes.d: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review of federal statutes.
trap_notes.default: United States v. Nixon limited executive privilege in criminal trials.

prompt: Identify this political science concept.
clues: It describes a three-way policy alliance in Washington that shapes federal rules.
The three corners are congressional committees, executive agencies, and interest groups.
Members trade campaign support, favorable budgets, and friendly regulations.

options.text: An iron triangle
A divided government
A party realignment
A closed party primary

explanation: Iron triangles connect congressional subcommittees, bureaucratic agencies, and interest groups in mutually beneficial policymaking.

trap_notes.b: Divided government occurs when different parties control the presidency and Congress.
trap_notes.c: Party realignment marks a lasting shift in voter coalitions between parties.
trap_notes.d: Winner-take-all primaries award all state delegates to the top candidate.
trap_notes.default: An iron triangle links congressional committees, agencies, and interest groups.

prompt: Identify this electoral system.
clues: It is widely used in European parliaments rather than U.S. congressional races.
Voters cast ballots for party lists in multi-member districts.
A party winning 20 percent of the vote receives roughly 20 percent of legislative seats.

options.text: Proportional representation
Single-member plurality
The Electoral College
Open-primary runoff

explanation: Proportional representation awards seats in line with vote shares, encouraging multi-party coalitions.

trap_notes.b: Single-member plurality awards each district seat solely to the top finisher.
trap_notes.c: The Electoral College is used only for U.S. presidential elections.
trap_notes.d: Runoff primaries select a single party nominee before a general election.
trap_notes.default: Proportional representation matches legislative seat shares to party vote shares.

prompt: Identify this international organization.
clues: Twelve Western nations founded this collective defense alliance in April 1949.
Its headquarters is in Brussels, Belgium, and it now includes over thirty members.
Article 5 of its treaty declares that an armed attack on one member is an attack on all.

options.text: North Atlantic Treaty Alliance
The World Trade Organization
The European Union bloc
The International Monetary Fund

explanation: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is a military alliance built on Article 5 collective defense.

trap_notes.b: The WTO regulates international trade rules and settles tariff disputes.
trap_notes.c: The European Union is a political and economic union, not a military alliance.
trap_notes.d: The IMF stabilizes exchange rates and lends to countries facing balance-of-payments crises.
trap_notes.default: NATO is a collective defense alliance anchored by Article 5.
